result: P. aeruginosa infection activates non-canonical inflammasomes (caspase-11/4 and GSDMD cleavage) but specifically inhibits downstream NLRP3 inflammasome activation (caspase-1 activation and IL-1β secretion) in both mouse and human macrophages.
evaluation: Claims C1-C11 provide converging evidence from immunoblotting (Figures 1A-B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-B) and ELISA assays (Figures 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) demonstrating normal upstream non-canonical inflammasome activation but inhibited downstream NLRP3 signaling. The pattern is consistent across mouse BMDM and human macrophages, with appropriate controls (E. coli comparison).

result: During P. aeruginosa infection, GSDMD-N localizes normally to mitochondrial membranes, mitochondrial DNA release is unaffected, and NUR77-NLRP3 binding is maintained, but NLRP3-NEK7 binding is significantly inhibited, suggesting a bacterial inhibitory factor acts specifically at the NLRP3-NEK7 interaction.
evaluation: Claims C12-C16 are supported by cellular fractionation (Figure 1F), PCR analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F), and co-immunoprecipitation experiments (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G-H). The data systematically rule out upstream defects and pinpoint NEK7 binding as the inhibited step, providing mechanistic insight into the site of bacterial interference.

result: Genetic dissection using Aim2, Gsdmd, and Casp11 knockout cells demonstrates that P. aeruginosa inhibition of NLRP3 requires caspase-11 but acts upstream of GSDMD, as NLRP3 inhibition persists in Gsdmd knockout cells but is relieved in Casp11 knockout cells.
evaluation: Claims C17-C26 present a logical genetic dissection using multiple knockout cell lines (Figures 1G-N, Figure 1—figure supplement 1I-L). The experiments systematically test the requirement for different inflammasome components and demonstrate that caspase-11 is necessary for the inhibitory effect. The experimental design is sound with appropriate controls, though the mechanism by which caspase-11 enables inhibition remains to be elucidated.

result: A systematic screening system identified VgrG1a and VgrG2b as caspase-11/4 substrates that can be cleaved by both mouse caspase-11 and human caspase-4 in an enzymatic activity-dependent manner, while other VgrG family members are not cleaved.
evaluation: Claims C27-C35 describe a novel screening approach (Figure 2A) validated by in vitro cleavage assays (Figures 2B-C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-L). The specificity is demonstrated by testing multiple VgrG family members. The screening system appears well-designed with appropriate positive and negative controls, though details about screening stringency and false positive/negative rates are not provided.

result: VgrG2b from the H2-T6SS secretion system enters macrophages during P. aeruginosa infection and is cleaved by caspase-11/4 in a caspase-dependent manner. VgrG2b-deficient P. aeruginosa no longer inhibits NLRP3 inflammasome activation, demonstrating that H2-T6SS-mediated VgrG2b delivery is essential for NLRP3 inhibition.
evaluation: Claims C36-C49 are supported by immunoblotting (Figures 2D-I), immunofluorescence (Figure 2E), genetic complementation experiments (Figures 2G-H), and VgrG2b knockout studies (Figures 2J-K). The data convincingly demonstrate VgrG2b entry into cells, caspase-dependent cleavage, and functional requirement for NLRP3 inhibition. The use of multiple approaches strengthens the conclusions.

result: VgrG2b is recognized by caspase-11/4 through binding to the p22/p10 complex, and the cleavage site is at aspartic acid 883 (D883) in the C-terminus, as demonstrated by site-directed mutagenesis showing that only the D883A mutant abolishes cleavage.
evaluation: Claims C50-C56 are supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments (Figures 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) and systematic mutagenesis (Figures 3B-C). The identification of D883 as the cleavage site is convincing through the use of point mutations. The data are consistent with known caspase-11 substrate recognition mechanisms.

result: The C-terminus of VgrG2b is both the binding site for caspase-11 recognition and contains the cleavage site, as demonstrated by chimeric protein experiments and direct binding assays showing C-terminal binding to caspase-11/4 p22/p10 complexes.
evaluation: Claims C57-C62 are supported by chimeric protein experiments (Figures 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B-C), co-immunoprecipitation (Figures 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), and in vitro cleavage assays (Figures 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E). The domain mapping approach is logical and the results are internally consistent.

result: VgrG2b cleavage at D883 by caspase-11 is crucial for NLRP3 inhibition, as P. aeruginosa carrying the D883A mutation no longer inhibits NLRP3 inflammasome activation or suppresses IL-1β secretion in both mouse and human macrophages, and this cleavage is specifically blocked by caspase-11 inhibitors but not caspase-3/7 inhibitors.
evaluation: Claims C63-C71 are supported by experiments with D883A mutant bacteria (Figures 3G-J, Figure 3—figure supplement 1G-I) and pharmacological inhibitor studies (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F). The data demonstrate functional importance of the cleavage site and specificity for caspase-11. The consistency across mouse and human systems strengthens the conclusions.

result: The cleaved C-terminus of VgrG2b specifically binds to NLRP3 (but not the N-terminus or full-length protein before cleavage), as demonstrated by yeast two-hybrid screening, co-immunoprecipitation in multiple cell types, and colocalization studies during P. aeruginosa infection.
evaluation: Claims C72-C80 are supported by yeast two-hybrid screening (Figure 4A), co-immunoprecipitation in HEK293T cells (Figures 4B-C), primary macrophages (Figures 4D-E), and immunofluorescence (Figure 4F). The use of multiple complementary approaches and demonstration in both overexpression and infection contexts provides strong evidence for the interaction.

result: VgrG2b C-terminus exhibits specific binding to NLRP3 at the NACHT-LRR junction and does not bind to other inflammasome components (GSDMD, ASC, or caspase-1), demonstrating high target specificity.
evaluation: Claims C81-C85 are supported by negative binding controls (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D-G) and domain mapping experiments (Figures 4G-I). The specificity testing is thorough and the identification of the NACHT-LRR junction as the binding site provides mechanistic detail. However, the binding affinity and stoichiometry are not quantified.

result: VgrG2b binding to NLRP3 requires caspase-11-mediated cleavage but is independent of NLRP3 activation status, as demonstrated by the absence of binding in Casp11 knockout cells but maintained binding in Gsdmd knockout cells where NLRP3 is not activated.
evaluation: Claims C86-C90 are supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments in knockout cell lines (Figures 4J, Figure 4—figure supplement 1H) and citations to prior literature (C88). The genetic dissection logically demonstrates that cleavage, not NLRP3 activation, is required for binding. This is an important mechanistic insight.

result: The metalloprotease activity of VgrG2b is not required for its cleavage by caspase-11 or its subsequent binding to and inhibition of NLRP3, as demonstrated by experiments with protease-inactive VgrG2b mutants.
evaluation: Claims C91-C94 are supported by experiments with VgrG2b protease mutants (Figure 4—figure supplement 1I-K). This control experiment is important for ruling out an alternative mechanism and demonstrating that the C-terminal fragment itself, not the protease activity, mediates NLRP3 inhibition.

result: VgrG2b C-terminus exhibits broad-spectrum inhibition of NLRP3 inflammasome activation in both canonical and non-canonical pathways across mouse and human cells, significantly reducing IL-1β secretion without affecting upstream caspase-11 and GSDMD activation.
evaluation: Claims C95-C102 are supported by experiments in HEK293T reconstitution systems (Figures 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), lentiviral overexpression (Figures 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), and cell-penetrating peptide delivery (Figures 5C-G, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C-F). The breadth of testing across different systems and stimuli is comprehensive.

result: VgrG2b C-terminus inhibits NLRP3 by specifically blocking NEK7 binding to NLRP3 through competitive binding to the same NLRP3 region, without affecting NLRP3's ATP hydrolysis activity or its binding to mitochondrial DNA or Nur77. VgrG2b-C has stronger binding affinity for NLRP3 than NEK7.
evaluation: Claims C103-C111 are supported by ATP hydrolysis assays (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G), co-immunoprecipitation experiments (Figures 5H-I, Figure 5—figure supplement 1H-J), and competitive binding studies (Figures 5J, Figure 5—figure supplement 1J). The mechanism is well-characterized through multiple complementary approaches. The competitive binding experiments convincingly demonstrate that VgrG2b-C outcompetes NEK7.

result: VgrG2b C-terminus does not inhibit the NLRC4 inflammasome, demonstrating specificity for NLRP3.
evaluation: Claim C112 is supported by immunoblotting data (Figure 5—figure supplement 1K). This specificity control is important for demonstrating that the inhibitory effect is NLRP3-specific and not a general inflammasome inhibitor.

result: In vivo infection with P. aeruginosa carrying the VgrG2b D883A mutation significantly improves mouse survival, increases IL-1β levels in serum and bronchoalveolar lavage fluid, reduces bacterial load in lungs, and restores NLRP3 inflammasome activation in lung macrophages, without affecting TNF-α or IL-6 levels.
evaluation: Claims C113-C119 are supported by mouse infection experiments with survival curves (Figure 6A), ELISA assays (Figures 6B-D, 6H-J), bacterial load quantification (Figure 6E), and inflammasome activation in BALF macrophages (Figure 6F). The in vivo data are consistent with in vitro findings and demonstrate physiological relevance. However, sample sizes appear small (n appears to be 4-6 based on data points) and statistical power may be limited.

result: A designed peptide mimicking VgrG2b C-terminus with a D883A mutation can competitively inhibit wild-type VgrG2b cleavage, relieve NLRP3 inhibition, increase IL-1β secretion in vitro, and when delivered to mouse lungs via nebulization, significantly improves survival and reduces bacterial load during P. aeruginosa infection.
evaluation: Claims C120-C128 are supported by in vitro experiments in mouse and human macrophages (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B-G) and in vivo mouse infection studies (Figures 6K-O). The therapeutic proof-of-concept is compelling, though C128's claim of 'potential medicinal value' is somewhat speculative. The peptide design is logical (TAT sequence for cell penetration, D883A to prevent cleavage, myristoylation for membrane targeting), but pharmacokinetic properties, optimal dosing, and long-term efficacy are not addressed.

result: Summary of main findings: VgrG2b from P. aeruginosa is cleaved by caspase-11 to generate a C-terminal fragment that binds NLRP3 and inhibits inflammasome activation and IL-1β secretion, and delivery of VgrG2b C-terminus mimics improves P. aeruginosa infection outcomes.
evaluation: Claims C129-C133 are summary statements supported by the collective evidence from all experiments throughout the manuscript. These represent the main conclusions of the study and are well-supported by the data.

result: Abstract summary claims about T6SS role in chronic infections, inflammasome importance in host defense, VgrG2b mechanism of NLRP3 inhibition via NEK7 displacement, and therapeutic peptide efficacy.
evaluation: Claims C134-C137 are abstract-level summary statements that accurately reflect the findings presented in the manuscript. C134-C135 are general knowledge claims supported by the literature, while C136-C137 summarize the key findings demonstrated in the results sections.

result: Background information about P. aeruginosa as an opportunistic pathogen, its secretion systems (T3SS and T6SS), the structure and function of T6SS components (H1-T6SS, H2-T6SS, H3-T6SS), and the role of VgrG2b in the T6SS.
evaluation: Claims C138-C156 are background/introduction claims supported by appropriate citations to the literature. These establish the context for the study and are accurately represented based on the cited references.

result: Background information about non-canonical inflammasomes, NLRP3 inflammasome activation mechanisms, the role of GSDMD, NEK7, and NUR77, LPS transport mechanisms, and the relationship between inflammasome obstruction and chronic infections.
evaluation: Claims C157-C172 are background/introduction claims supported by appropriate citations to the literature. These provide the immunological context for understanding the significance of the findings.

result: Discussion points about VgrG2b serving as both a delivery protein and a virulence factor that requires cleavage, the novelty of this hijacking mechanism, caspase substrate recognition mechanisms, and the dual function of VgrG2b in transporting virulence factors and inhibiting NLRP3.
evaluation: Claims C173-C183 are discussion/interpretation statements that are supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript. These represent reasonable interpretations of the findings, though some (C179, C180, C181) involve broader generalizations about pathogen strategies that extend beyond the specific data presented.
